dialog.body: Public Works, storm line, this is Lorraine. What can I do for you this afternoon?
Hi, yeah. Before anything, sorry, can I get your name again? I'm writing this down. Your last name too, if that's okay.
Sure. Lorraine Medeiros. M-E-D-E-I-R-O-S.

M-E-D... E-I-R-O-S. Okay. And it's, uh, two forty-three, Sunday. Got it. So my name is Diogo Resendes. I'm calling about the storm drain at the corner by my parents' house. Fourteen Wellington Avenue. This is, I want to say, my fourth time calling about this drain this winter between me and my father. Fourth time.
Okay, Fourteen Wellington Avenue. Resendes. Hold on, let me pull it up. [pause] Yeah, I've got the address. Actually I think I talked to your father back in January. Carlos?

That's him, yeah. Okay, so you know the history. Good. That saves some time. So this storm, the nor'easter, came in yesterday, wrapped up this morning, and the drain backed up again. Same exact thing. The whole corner turned into a pond.
Okay. So the drain at the corner backed up again during this storm. How bad did it get out there?

Ankle deep. On the street. I went out there around, I wrote it down, around seven this morning, and it was over my ankles at the curb. It came up to the top step out front. And cars were going through it like boats. Throwing wakes, right up onto the sidewalk, up onto the steps. One guy in a pickup just plowed right through and the water went halfway up the front walk.
Ankle deep at the curb, up to the top step, and cars throwing wakes up onto the sidewalk. Okay, I'm putting all that in. And the house, did any water get inside this time?

No. And that's, I mean, that's the only good news. The basement stayed dry this time. Completely dry, I checked it twice, I checked it again before I called you. But that's luck. That's not anything anybody did. It just didn't rain as long, or the tide wasn't the same, I don't know. Because the street did the exact same thing it did both other times.
Okay. Basement stayed dry this storm. I'm glad about that, at least.

Yeah. Me too. But see, it flooded twice already this winter. Once after the January storm, the coastal one, that's when my father called you, and then again after the snow that turned to rain, end of January, that's when I called. Two times. And both times it started the same way, the corner backs up, the street fills, and then it's in the house. So this morning I'm standing at the window watching the water climb up the steps thinking, here we go, round three. It didn't happen. But it could've.

I hear you. Let me read back what I have so far so I've got it right. Corner drain near Fourteen Wellington backed up during the nor'easter, the one that came in Saturday. Street ponded about ankle deep, up to the top step, cars pushing water up onto the sidewalk. No water in the basement this time. Basement flooded twice earlier this winter, once after the January coastal storm and once after the snow-to-rain storm. That sound right?

That's right. That's all right. Okay. [pause] Sorry, I'm, uh, I'm walking around. I got one of those standing desks a while back so now I just pace the whole time I'm on the phone. My wife says I wear a track in the floor. Anyway.
That's alright, pace away.

So here's my thing. Okay. After the first time, a crew came, that Wednesday, and they cleaned off the grate and shoveled some silt out of the top. That's it. Then it flooded again. Then a crew came on the twenty-eighth and jetted the line and told us, told my father, it was partly blocked. Partly blocked. Then a supervisor called me, said it's going on the engineering review. Then I called back, a supervisor called me again on, uh, February second, I have it right here, and said they're looking at a bigger fix. No date. That was three weeks ago. And today the street's a lake again. So what happened with the engineering review?

Okay. I can see the two crew visits in here, the fourteenth and the twenty-eighth, and I see the note that it was flagged for engineering. What I don't see is anything after that. There's no work order for a bigger job on there yet, no date.
Right. No date. That's what they told me three weeks ago. Nothing's changed.
I know. I'm sorry. I'm on the storm line today so I don't have the engineering folks here, it's just us on a Sunday. But I can put this backup into the file so it's on record with the other ones.
Hold on. Can you, so, I'm writing. You're adding it to... what's it called, the file?
It's the repeat backup file for that location. So everything's together. The January calls, the crew visits, and now today.

Repeat backup file. Okay. [pause] And then what? Because honestly, Lorraine, I don't mean anything against you, you've been very nice, but I've had a lot of people tell me it's noted. Noted, flagged, it's on the list. And then I'm standing in ankle-deep water on a Sunday morning watching a pickup truck send a wave at my parents' front door.

No, that's fair. I'm also going to send a message to the supervisor directly, tonight, so it's not just sitting in the file. That this location backed up again in this storm, the street ponded, and that it's the third time this winter the drain's backed up even though the house stayed dry this time.
Okay. That's good. That's, yeah. Supervisor directly. [line breaks up] ...and when would...
Sorry, you cut out there. When would what?
Sorry, I'm in the kitchen, the signal's terrible in here. I said when would somebody actually come out. Is a crew coming tomorrow, or?

I can't book a crew from this line for this one, because it's already in front of the supervisor and engineering. So I don't have a new crew date for you. The supervisor will see the message first thing tomorrow, and they're the one who'd send somebody or call you.
So no crew date.
No crew date from me today, no.

[pause] Okay. Okay. I'm writing that down. No crew date. Supervisor gets message Monday morning. [pause] Can I ask you something else, then? Because I've been going back and forth on this. Whose drain is it, actually? Is that the city's or is that the state? Because somebody at my work said if it's near a state road it's the state's problem and the city can't touch it, and I thought, well, maybe that's why nothing's happening. Maybe I've been calling the wrong people for six weeks.

I understand why you'd ask. Wellington's a city street, and that basin's in our system. Our crews are the ones that went out there both times, you can see it right here in the log. So as far as I can see, it's ours.
It's yours. City.

That's what our records show. If engineering finds out something different when they look at the line, like it ties into something that isn't ours, they'd be the ones to tell you that. But the basin on the corner, that's been us.
Okay. Well, at least that's clear. City. [crosstalk]
Go ahead.
No, go ahead, sorry.
I was just going to ask, is the water still out there now, or has it gone down?

It's going down. It's slow. When I looked about an hour ago there was still a big puddle at the curb, maybe a couple inches, and the grate's got all this junk on it. Leaves, sand, a coffee cup. I didn't touch it. Last time somebody told my father not to mess with the grate, so.
Yeah, don't go poking at it, especially with traffic going by. I'll put in that there's still standing water at the curb and debris on the grate as of this afternoon.

Thank you. And can you put in that the crew that jetted it said it was partly blocked? Because to me, partly blocked means there's still something down there. They didn't say they cleared it. They said partly blocked. I wrote it down when my father told me.
It's already in the crew note from the twenty-eighth, but I'll put it in my message to the supervisor too, so they see it right alongside today.

Okay. Good. [pause] I'm sorry, I'm just... my parents are in their seventies. My father's seventy-seven. Every time it rains now he's up all night going down those stairs to check. And I'm over here, I'm checking the weather app every hour like it's my job. And every time I call it's very polite, very nice, and then the next storm comes and it's the same corner doing the same thing.
I get it. I really do. I'll tell you, I wrote down your father's call myself back in January, so I remember this one. It's not just a number to me.

I appreciate that. I do. Okay. So let me read back what I have, make sure I've got everything. [line breaks up] ...Lorraine Medeiros, storm line, Sunday the twenty-second. Backup added to the repeat backup file. Message to the supervisor tonight. Supervisor sees it Monday. No crew date. Drain is the city's. Is that everything?

Sorry, the beginning cut out, but what I caught is right. Repeat backup file, message to the supervisor tonight, no crew date from me, and the basin's ours. And I noted the house stayed dry this time and the street ponded up to the steps.
Okay. Do you need a number for me? The supervisor's called me before.
I see you're already on here as the contact, from the last couple of calls. I'll put you down as the person to call back.
Good. Yeah, me, not my father. He's had enough of the phone with this.
Got it. You as the contact.
And if I don't hear anything by, say, Wednesday, what do I do? Call this number again, or the regular one?
The regular Public Works line during the week. Tell them it's the repeat backup at Fourteen Wellington and ask for the supervisor. They'll find it fast.

Regular line, during the week, repeat backup at Fourteen Wellington, ask for the supervisor. Okay. [pause] I called this one because it's Sunday and City Hall's closed, obviously. I figured there's no point waiting till tomorrow and calling with a bunch of other people after the storm. But I almost didn't call at all, honestly, because I thought, what's the point, it's the same answer.
I'm glad you did call. If it isn't written down after every storm, it looks like it only happened twice. This way there's a record it keeps happening.
Yeah. Keeps happening. That's the whole problem. [inaudible] ...next week.
I missed that last part, sorry.
I said they're talking about more rain next week. So, you know. I'd like somebody to actually look at it before then. Not after.
I'll put that in too, that there's rain in the forecast and you're asking for it to be looked at before the next one.
Okay. Thank you, Lorraine. Really. I know it's not you holding this up.
You're welcome. Hope the rest of your Sunday's drier than the morning was.
Yeah. We'll see. Okay, bye.
Bye now.
